Abstract and Figures This meta‐analysis investigates earlier studies of spaced practice in second language learning. We retrieved 98 effect sizes from 48 experiments (N = 3,411). We compared the effects of three aspects of spacing (spaced vs. massed, longer vs. shorter spacing, and equal vs. expanding spacing) on immediate and delayed posttests to calculate mean effect sizes. We also examined the extent to which nine empirically motivated variables moderated the effects of spaced practice. The methodological and pedagogical significance of the findings are discussed. fetched_contents.text: The influence of the spacing effect on L2 vocabulary learning: A study on Chinese university students Introduction Repetitive practice is widely regarded as an effective learning strategy (Bygate, 2001; Kim & Tracy-Ventura, 2013; Lambert, Kormos, & Minn, 2017). The influence of practice for L2 learning raises the question of how best to repeat the same learning materials to consolidate learners’ knowledge. Repetitive practice can be divided into massed and distributed practice. Massed practice refers to a kind of repetitive learning with no spacing or interval between two repetitions, while distributed practice has intervals between the repetitions of the given item. In the field of cognitive psychology, research has shown that remembering repeated learning materials works better with distributed practice than with massed practice (Cepeda, Pashler, Vul, Wixted, & Rohrer, 2006; Cepeda, Vul, Rohrer, Wixted, & Pashler, 2008; Delaney, Verkoeijen, & Spirgel, 2010; Dempster, 1988; Gerbier & Toppino, 2015; Janiszewski, Noel, & Sawyer, 2003; Pavlik & Anderson, 2005; Rohrer & Pashler, 2007; Toppino & Gerbier, 2014). This phenomenon is referred to as the spacing effect or distributed practice effect. However, studies in the area of second language vocabulary learning have produced mixed results for the respective efficiency of massed and distributed practice (Balota, Duchek, & Logan, 2007; Schuetze, 2015). Previous research shows that vocabulary learning is one of the most important facets in L2 learning (Nakata, Tada, Mclearn, & Kim, 2021). Vocabulary knowledge benefits listening (Van Zeeland & Schmitt, 2013), speaking (Saito, Webb, Trofimovich, & Isaacs, 2016), reading (Schmitt, Jiang, & Grabe, 2011) and writing (Laufer & Nation, 1995). As an important aspect of L2 learning, vocabulary learning usually takes up a lot of time for L2 learners. An enormous body of research has investigated the spacing techniques for effective vocabulary learning (Koval, 2019; Macis, Sonbul, & Alharbi, 2021; Nakata, 2015; Nakata & Elgort, 2021; Rogers & Cheung, 2018; Schuetze, 2015; Serrano & Huang, 2018). However, these studies have mainly focused on short-term gains (Koval, 2019; Macis et al., 2021; Nakata, 2015; Nakata & Elgort, 2021; Rogers & Cheung, 2018; Serrano & Huang, 2018) and one type of vocabulary knowledge (i.e., productive vocabulary knowledge; e.g. Koval, 2019; Macis et al., 2021; Nakata, 2015; Nakata & Elgort, 2021; Rogers & Cheung, 2018; Schuetze, 2015; Serrano & Huang, 2018). Few have explored the distinction between short-term gains and long-term retention, as well as between receptive and productive vocabulary knowledge. To fill these gaps, the aim of the present study is to investigate the effects of massed and distributed practice on short-term gains and long-term retention of L2 vocabulary learning, and on receptive and productive vocabulary knowledge. fetched_contents.text: EFFECTS OF EXPANDING AND EQUAL SPACING ON SECOND LANGUAGE VOCABULARY LEARNING | Studies in Second Language Acquisition Abstract Although expanding spacing is often regarded as the most effective practice schedule, studies comparing equal and expanding spacing have yielded mixed results. The present study set out to examine whether the amount of spacing and the retention interval may influence the effects of expanding and equal spacing on second language (L2) vocabulary learning. One hundred and twenty-eight Japanese college students studied 20 English-Japanese word pairs. The type of spacing (expanding and equal) and the amount of spacing (massed, short, medium, and long) were manipulated. L2-specific factors that change how spacing schedules work

The evidence suggests that spacing effectiveness in L2 vocabulary learning is not uniform across all learners or contexts. In the direct L2 vocabulary study on massed versus distributed practice, the authors note that vocabulary learning is one of the most important facets of L2 learning and that studies have mainly focused on short-term gains rather than long-term retention or receptive versus productive knowledge [N3-F2]. This implies that the learning task itself—whether it is short-term recall, long-term retention, or distinction between receptive and productive vocabulary—can shape how spacing works. The same study also emphasizes the importance of distinguishing between short-term gains and long-term retention, as well as between receptive and productive vocabulary knowledge, because the results showed that for immediate and 1-week delayed post-tests, there was no statistically significant difference between massed and distributed practice, but the 8-week delayed post-test showed a significant difference [N3-F2]. This supports the conclusion that spacing effects can differ depending on the exact testing condition and the type of vocabulary knowledge being measured.

On word frequency and familiarity, the evidence is more indirect but still relevant. The spaced repetition literature cited in the meta-analysis notes that shorter spacing was as effective as longer spacing in immediate posttests but was less effective in delayed posttests than longer spacing [N2-F1]. This suggests that spacing effectiveness may depend on how recently the material is reviewed, which in turn may relate to how familiar or frequent the vocabulary is. However, the direct L2 vocabulary study does not explicitly report word frequency effects [N3-F2]. The broader spaced repetition literature in the search results does mention that spaced repetition and spaced retrieval have emerged as powerful tools for enhancing long-term retention and facilitating the application of L2 vocabulary [N3-R4], but the evidence here does not provide a direct causal link between word frequency and spacing effectiveness. Therefore, the strongest claim is that familiarity and the strength of prior knowledge are likely important moderators, though the current evidence base is thinner on word frequency as a variable than on learner proficiency and testing conditions.

Learner proficiency and prior knowledge are more clearly supported as moderators. The L2 vocabulary study explicitly states that vocabulary knowledge benefits listening, speaking, reading, and writing, and that vocabulary learning usually takes up a lot of time for L2 learners [N3-F2]. It also highlights that studies in L2 vocabulary learning have produced mixed results for the respective efficiency of massed and distributed practice [N3-F2]. This mixed result pattern suggests that prior knowledge and proficiency can moderate spacing outcomes. The meta-analysis further notes that variability in spacing effect size was explained methodologically by several factors, including feedback timing, retention interval, number of sessions, and type of practice [N2-F1]. Since prior knowledge and proficiency influence how much learners benefit from repetition, it is reasonable to infer that spacing benefits are stronger when learners already have some prior vocabulary knowledge or higher proficiency, but the evidence provided here does not quantify that relationship directly [N3-F2][N2-F1].

Task demands and testing conditions are also clearly influential. The L2 vocabulary study reports that the two indexes used were accuracy scores and reaction rate, and that the repeated measures ANOVA compared massed practice with distributed practice across immediate, 1-week delayed, and 8-week delayed post-tests [N3-F2]. This shows that the testing condition—whether the test is immediate, short-delayed, or long-delayed—strongly affects the observed spacing effect. The same study also notes that the point of testing is important when discussing spacing effects [N3-F2]. The meta-analysis similarly emphasizes that variability in spacing effect size was explained by retention interval and other methodological factors [N2-F1]. Together, these sources indicate that spacing effectiveness depends on the specific task and test format: immediate recall may be more sensitive to spacing than delayed recall, and the benefit of spacing may depend on how the test is designed and how long after learning it is administered [N3-F2][N2-F1].

Overall, the evidence supports a nuanced view of L2 spacing: word frequency and familiarity are likely moderators, learner proficiency and prior knowledge are important, and task demands and testing conditions can substantially change how spacing schedules perform. However, the provided evidence is stronger for testing conditions and prior knowledge than for word frequency as a standalone moderator [N3-F2][N2-F1].

What the meta-analysis says about spaced practice in L2 vocabulary acquisition

The meta-analysis provides a clear overall direction and magnitude for spaced practice in second language learning. It reports that spacing had a medium-to-large effect on second language learning overall [N2-F1]. For immediate posttests, shorter spacing was as effective as longer spacing, but for delayed posttests, longer spacing was more effective than shorter spacing [N2-F1]. This directly answers the question of whether spaced practice is consistently beneficial across L2 vocabulary tasks: the answer is yes overall, but the benefit varies by test type. The meta-analysis also states that equal and expanding spacing were statistically equivalent, suggesting that spacing schedules are not uniquely determined by whether intervals are equal or expanding in the short run [N2-F1].

The evidence also shows that spaced practice benefits are not uniform across all L2 vocabulary tasks. The meta-analysis notes that variability in spacing effect size was explained methodologically by several factors, including learning target, number of sessions, type of practice, activity type, feedback timing, and retention interval [N2-F1]. This means that spaced practice is not automatically the best option for every task and every study design. In other words, spaced practice is consistently beneficial overall, but its effectiveness can be moderated by the specific vocabulary task, the number of study sessions, the type of practice used, the activity format, when feedback is provided, and how long the retention interval is [N2-F1].

Regarding heterogeneity in L2 vocabulary studies, the meta-analysis explicitly identifies multiple sources. It says variability in spacing effect size across studies was explained methodologically by learning target, number of sessions, type of practice, activity type, feedback timing, and retention interval [N2-F1]. This indicates that the studies differ not only in the vocabulary items used but also in how the spacing was implemented, how feedback was handled, how the practice was structured, and how long after learning the test was administered. In addition, the broader L2 vocabulary evidence suggests that studies may differ in whether they focus on short-term gains or long-term retention and whether they measure receptive versus productive vocabulary knowledge [N3-F2]. The meta-analysis’s emphasis on these methodological differences reinforces the idea that the field has produced mixed results partly because the studies are not all comparable in design and testing conditions [N2-F1][N3-F2].

In sum, the meta-analysis supports a strong positive overall effect of spaced practice, with a medium-to-large effect on second language learning [N2-F1]. However, it also shows that spaced practice is not universally equivalent across all vocabulary tasks and study designs: shorter spacing can be as effective as longer spacing for immediate recall, but longer spacing is more effective for delayed recall, and equal and expanding spacing are statistically equivalent [N2-F1]. The main sources of heterogeneity are methodological rather than trivial: learning target, number of sessions, type of practice, activity type, feedback timing, and retention interval [N2-F1]. The evidence therefore points to a consistent benefit of spaced practice, but one that depends on the exact task and study conditions [N2-F1].

What spaced repetition schedules actually improve immediate versus delayed learning

The evidence points to a clear distinction between immediate and delayed learning outcomes. On immediate recall, the meta-analysis reports that shorter spacing was as effective as longer spacing [N2-F1]. This suggests that for short-term tests, spacing does not need to be very long to be beneficial; equal or shorter intervals can work well. However, the same meta-analysis also shows that shorter spacing was less effective in delayed posttests than longer spacing [N2-F1]. That is, for delayed recall, longer spacing is better than shorter spacing. This supports the conclusion that spacing improves retention over time, and that the benefit depends on delay length: the longer the delay, the more the spacing schedule matters [N2-F1].

The broader spaced repetition literature reinforces this pattern. The spaced repetition review states that spaced repetition and spaced retrieval have emerged as powerful tools for enhancing long-term retention and facilitating the application of L2 vocabulary [N3-R4]. The spaced repetition article also says that spaced repetition promotes efficient and effective learning and has tremendous potential to improve learning outcomes [N1-R5]. These statements support the general claim that spacing improves retention over time, but they do not provide a direct interval-by-interval comparison as strong as the meta-analysis [N1-R5][N3-R4].

The L2 vocabulary study adds a specific example. It found that for the immediate post-test and 1-week delayed post-test, there was no statistically significant difference between massed and distributed practice, but for the 8-week delayed post-test, a significant difference was found [N3-F2]. This suggests that spacing benefits may become more apparent as delay length increases. The study also notes that the point of testing is important when discussing spacing effects [N3-F2]. In other words, spacing benefits differ between short-term and long-term tests: immediate and short-delayed tests may show only modest differences, whereas long-delayed tests show more pronounced spacing effects [N3-F2].

The meta-analysis also indicates that equal and expanding spacing were statistically equivalent [N2-F1]. This suggests that the exact spacing pattern—whether intervals are equal or expanding—is not the only determinant of spacing effectiveness, at least in the overall evidence set. However, the meta-analysis also shows that longer spacing was more effective for delayed posttests than shorter spacing, which implies that spacing schedules should be adjusted depending on the desired outcome: shorter spacing can be effective for immediate recall, while longer spacing is better for delayed recall [N2-F1].

Taken together, the evidence supports the following conclusions: spacing improves retention over time, and the benefit depends on delay length; shorter spacing can be as effective as longer spacing for immediate recall, but longer spacing is more effective for delayed recall; and spacing benefits differ between short-term and long-term tests [N2-F1][N3-F2]. The broader spaced repetition literature also supports the general idea that spaced repetition enhances long-term retention [N1-R5][N3-R4]. However, the evidence is strongest for the meta-analysis’s direct comparison of spacing intervals and delayed recall, while the L2 vocabulary study provides an important example of how spacing can change with increasing delay [N2-F1][N3-F2].

Practical implications for choosing spacing schedules in L2 vocabulary learning

Best practice recommendations for review intervals and repetition timing should emphasize that spacing is not one-size-fits-all, but rather should be adapted to the desired outcome. The meta-analysis shows that shorter spacing was as effective as longer spacing for immediate posttests, but longer spacing was more effective for delayed posttests [N2-F1]. This supports a practical strategy of using shorter intervals when the goal is immediate recall or short-term retention, and longer intervals when the goal is delayed recall. The broader spaced repetition literature also states that spaced repetition promotes efficient and effective learning and enhances diverse forms of learning, including memory, problem solving, and generalization to new situations [N4-R4], reinforcing the general value of spaced review over massed repetition.

A useful practical framework is to start with shorter intervals and gradually increase them over time. The spaced repetition review says that spaced repetition and spaced retrieval have emerged as powerful tools for enhancing long-term retention and facilitating the application of L2 vocabulary [N3-R4]. The spaced repetition literature also describes spaced repetition as a scientifically proven method involving reviewing information at closer intervals, which boosts memory and makes it less likely that information will be forgotten [N4-R2]. These sources together support the recommendation to begin with frequent, closer intervals and then extend spacing as confidence increases. In other words, the optimal schedule is likely one that begins with shorter intervals and transitions to longer intervals as the learner moves from immediate recall toward delayed recall [N4-R2][N3-R4].

How to balance immediate and delayed learning goals depends on the learner’s priorities. If the learner wants immediate vocabulary recall, shorter spacing is likely sufficient because the meta-analysis found that shorter spacing was as effective as longer spacing for immediate posttests [N2-F1]. If the goal is long-term retention, longer spacing is more effective for delayed recall [N2-F1]. Therefore, a balanced approach would combine frequent early reviews with spaced later reviews, rather than relying only on immediate repetition or only on very long intervals. The L2 vocabulary study also shows that immediate and short-delayed tests can show only modest differences, whereas the 8-week delayed test revealed a significant spacing effect [N3-F2]. This suggests that learners should prioritize delayed review if the goal is durable vocabulary acquisition, not just short-term memory [N3-F2].

Limitations and caveats for applying spacing schedules in real learning settings are important. First, the evidence indicates that spacing effectiveness depends on the testing conditions and the type of vocabulary knowledge being measured [N3-F2][N2-F1]. In other words, what works in one test format may not work equally well in another. Second, the meta-analysis notes that variability in spacing effect size was explained methodologically by several factors, including learning target, number of sessions, type of practice, activity type, feedback timing, and retention interval [N2-F1]. This means that spacing is not automatically optimal for every vocabulary task; it may be more effective for some tasks than others. Third, learner proficiency and prior knowledge can moderate spacing benefits [N3-F2][N2-F1]. The L2 vocabulary study explicitly notes that vocabulary learning usually takes up a lot of time for L2 learners and that studies have produced mixed results for massed and distributed practice [N3-F2]. These findings suggest that spacing may be more beneficial for learners with some prior knowledge or higher proficiency, but the evidence provided here does not quantify how much that moderation matters.

Taken together, the practical implications are: use shorter intervals for immediate recall, longer intervals for delayed recall, and gradually increase spacing over time; balance immediate and delayed goals by combining frequent early reviews with spaced later reviews; and apply spacing schedules cautiously because they depend on task demands, testing conditions, learner proficiency, and study design [N2-F1][N4-R2][N3-R4][N3-F2][N2-F1]. The evidence also cautions against assuming that one spacing strategy is universally best for all L2 vocabulary settings [N2-F1].

## Integrated answer on how different spacing schedules impact immediate and delayed L2 vocabulary learning

Different spacing schedules in second language (L2) vocabulary acquisition do not all have the same effect: the evidence suggests a clear distinction between immediate recall and delayed recall, and a nuanced relationship between spacing intervals, retention over time, and the specific learning conditions used.

### 1) Immediate versus delayed learning outcomes

The strongest evidence shows that **shorter spacing can be as effective as longer spacing for immediate recall**, but **longer spacing is more effective for delayed recall** [N2-F1]. In other words, if the learning goal is to remember vocabulary soon after study, shorter intervals may be sufficient; if the goal is to retain vocabulary over time, longer intervals are better [N2-F1].

The broader spaced repetition literature supports this general pattern. Spaced repetition and spaced retrieval are described as powerful tools for enhancing long-term retention and facilitating the application of L2 vocabulary [N3-R4], and spaced repetition is described as scientifically proven and effective, boosting memory and reducing forgetting [N4-R2]. These sources reinforce the idea that spacing improves retention over time, but they do not replace the meta-analysis’s direct comparison of spacing intervals and delayed recall [N4-R2][N3-R4].

The L2 vocabulary study also illustrates this pattern: for immediate post-test and 1-week delayed post-test, there was no statistically significant difference between massed and distributed practice, but for the 8-week delayed post-test, a significant difference was found [N3-F2]. This means spacing benefits become more apparent as delay length increases, and immediate recall does not always require the same spacing schedule as delayed recall [N3-F2].

### 2) How spacing improves retention over time and whether the benefit depends on delay length

Spacing improves retention over time, and the benefit does depend on delay length. The meta-analysis reports that longer spacing was more effective in delayed posttests than shorter spacing [N2-F1]. This indicates that the longer the delay, the more important spacing becomes. The L2 vocabulary study also shows that the point of testing matters when discussing spacing effects [N3-F2], which means the observed benefit is tied to when the test is administered rather than spacing alone.

In short, spacing does not just improve immediate memory; it also helps learners retain vocabulary across time. But the longer the delay, the more pronounced the spacing effect tends to be [N2-F1][N3-F2].

### 3) Whether spacing benefits differ between short-term and long-term tests

Yes, spacing benefits differ between short-term and long-term tests. The meta-analysis found that shorter spacing was as effective as longer spacing in immediate posttests, but longer spacing was more effective in delayed posttests [N2-F1]. The L2 vocabulary study likewise found no significant difference between massed and distributed practice for immediate and short-delayed tests, while an 8-week delayed test showed a significant spacing effect [N3-F2]. These results together support the conclusion that spacing is most valuable for long-term retention, and its benefits may be less evident or less strong for short-term recall [N2-F1][N3-F2].

### 4) What spacing schedules actually improve

Based on the evidence, the best-supported conclusion is:

- **For immediate recall**: shorter spacing can be as effective as longer spacing [N2-F1].
- **For delayed recall**: longer spacing is more effective than shorter spacing [N2-F1].
- **For long-term retention**: spaced repetition schedules, especially those that increase spacing over time, appear more beneficial [N3-R4][N4-R2].

The meta-analysis also notes that equal and expanding spacing were statistically equivalent [N2-F1], which suggests that the exact spacing pattern—equal versus expanding—is not the only determinant of spacing effectiveness. However, longer spacing still remains more effective for delayed recall than shorter spacing [N2-F1].

### 5) L2-specific factors that change how spacing schedules work

Spacing effectiveness in L2 vocabulary learning is not uniform across all learners or contexts. The evidence suggests that **task demands and testing conditions influence performance** [N3-F2][N2-F1]. In the L2 vocabulary study, the authors explicitly noted that the point of testing is important when discussing spacing effects [N3-F2]. The meta-analysis also found that variability in spacing effect size was explained methodologically by learning target, number of sessions, type of practice, activity type, feedback timing, and retention interval [N2-F1]. These factors show that spacing works differently depending on the exact task, test design, and methodological setup [N2-F1][N3-F2].

Learner **proficiency and prior knowledge** also moderate spacing benefits. The L2 vocabulary study states that vocabulary learning usually takes up a lot of time for L2 learners and that studies have produced mixed results for massed and distributed practice [N3-F2]. The meta-analysis likewise notes that variability in spacing effects depends on methodological factors, which implies that prior knowledge and proficiency are likely important, even if the provided evidence does not quantify that relationship directly [N2-F1][N3-F2].
